title: Derivative Complexity and Stock Price Crash Risk: Evidence from China
content: This study examines whether the complexity of derivative use affects stock price crash risk in China’s capital market. Using a novel hand-collected dataset based on annual reports of A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2016, we develop multidimensional indicators capturing both the economic and accounting complexity of derivative positions. The analysis reveals that greater complexity is associated with a significantly lower likelihood of stock price crashes. This mitigating effect is particularly evident in non-state-owned enterprises, firms with weaker internal control systems, and those operating in more transparent information environments. Robustness checks, including treatment effect models and propensity score matching, confirm the reliability of the results. These findings suggest that derivative complexity, when accompanied by transparent disclosure, can enhance information quality and reduce downside risk. This research contributes to the literature on corporate derivatives and crash risk by providing the first large-scale evidence from an emerging market context. It also offers important implications for regulators, investors, and financial reporting practices in environments with limited governance strength.
